title: Newman's reduction preserves approximate correctness
statement: Let $\Omega$ be a finite probability space, let $X$ and $Y$ be finite types, and let $p$ be a public-coin finite-message protocol over shared randomness $\Omega$ with inputs in $X$ and $Y$ and outputs in a type $\alpha$. Fix a target function $f : X \times Y \to \alpha$, a real error bound $\varepsilon$, and a real constant $c > 1$, and suppose that $p$ $\varepsilon$-computes $f$, meaning that for every input pair $(x,y)$ the probability over the shared randomness that $p$ outputs something other than $f(x,y)$ is at most $\varepsilon$. Then the associated Newman protocol — the private-coin protocol in which Alice draws an index into the fixed table of good random seeds, sends it to Bob, and both run $p$ deterministically on that seed — $(c\varepsilon)$-computes $f$: for every input pair $(x,y)$ the probability over the private randomness that its output differs from $f(x,y)$ is at most $c\varepsilon$.
hypotheses_covered: Ω is a finite probability space
p is a public-coin finite-message protocol over Ω
f : X → Y → α is the target function
ε and c are real parameters
replaced:
If $p$ is a public-coin finite-message protocol that $\varepsilon$-computes $f$, and $c > 1$,
then the Newman protocol $(p.\mathtt{newmanProtocol}\;f\;\varepsilon\;c)$
is a private-coin protocol that $(c \cdot \varepsilon)$-computes $f$, i.e.\
for all inputs $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ the probability that the protocol's output
differs from $f(x, y)$ is at most $c \cdot \varepsilon$.
